Pop Art. A mid-twentieth-century movement that elevated mass-produced consumer imagery, advertising, comic books, and popular culture to the status of fine art. Pop Art emerged simultaneously in Britain and America in the nineteen-fifties and sixties, embracing rather than critiquing commercial aesthetics.

The movement reacted against Abstract Expressionism's emotional intensity and elite pretension by celebrating everyday commercial imagery with cool detachment and deadpan technique. Key artists include Andy Warhol, who worked with commercial iconography and mass production and celebrity images; Roy Lichtenstein, who enlarged comic strips; James Rosenquist, who employed billboard techniques; and Claes Oldenburg, who created giant soft sculptures of consumer goods.

Pop Art employed mechanical reproduction techniques—silkscreen printing, commercial offset processes, bold primary colors—to deliberately blur the distinction between hand-made art and industrial manufacturing, eroding artistic mystique. The movement embraced repetition and serialization as philosophical statements, mirroring the sameness of mass production and the infinitude of consumer desire through serialized imagery.

The iconography was drawn from supermarket shelves, advertising, Hollywood, and disaster. Campbell's Soup Cans, Elvis, car crashes—artists treated banal commercial subjects with the reverence once reserved for classical mythology. Deeply ironic, Pop Art remains debated: whether it celebrates or critiques consumer culture, likely doing both simultaneously. Complicity and critique become indistinguishable. Its embrace of mass media and commercial aesthetics presaged contemporary art's complicated relationship to advertising, celebrity culture, and digital reproduction, anticipating the internet age and postmodern pastiche.
